The community centre smelled of floor cleaner and marigolds. Chandrika sat behind the voter-registration desk with a stack of forms, checking her phone every few minutes. Two weeks ago she had promised Abhinav she would run the stall so he could be at his grandmother's eightieth birthday in another town.
At ten her hostel group had messaged: a spare pass to the music festival, front section, leaving in an hour. Her thumb hovered. She could call Abhinav, say something had come up. He would understand. Probably.
She typed, "Can't, covering for someone," and put the phone face down. By four she had helped thirty-one first-time voters fill in their forms. A photo arrived from Abhinav: a cake, a grinning old lady, and "Thank you, I owe you big." She looked at it for a long time.

qa.q: How many first-time voters had Chandrika helped by four?
qa.a: She had helped thirty-one first-time voters fill in their forms.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling when her thumb hovered over the phone?
qa.a: She felt torn between wanting the festival pass and her promise to Abhinav, and was tempted to invent an excuse.

qa.q: Which choice did Chandrika make, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She turned down the pass and stayed at the desk, which kept her word and makes her someone Abhinav can rely on.

qa.q: What did Chandrika's staying mean for Abhinav?
qa.a: It let him celebrate his grandmother's eightieth birthday without worry, which is why he wrote, "Thank you, I owe you big."

grounding: A young woman keeps her promise to cover a stall even when a more exciting offer appears, feeling the pull of desire against duty.

Uday,
I know you're annoyed, so I'm writing properly instead of sending a sticker.
Yes, the beach trip sounds perfect, and yes, I was the one who pushed for it last year. But in March I promised Ma I'd be home the week after her knee operation, to do the cooking and drive her to the check-up. It's the same week.
I'll be honest: I spent two days thinking of ways to wriggle out. Ma would have said, "Go, beta, I'll manage." That's exactly why I can't. She'd manage by struggling up and down the stairs.
So I'm staying. It stings, especially knowing I'll see the group photos. Keep a seat for me on the next trip, and don't eat all the fried fish without me.
Vikas

On Tuesday morning, in her rented flat in Mumbai, Aparna looked at her calendar and felt her stomach drop. She had promised Hrithik she would build the website for his tiffin service by Friday. Her office had just moved her project deadline to Thursday.
She could keep quiet and hope, or send a vague "something came up" on Friday night. Instead she called him before nine.
"Hrithik, I can't finish the full site by Friday. I'm sorry; I know you planned the launch around it." He was quiet. "What I can do: the home page and menu by Friday, so you can launch, and the order form by next Wednesday. If that doesn't work, I'll connect you with someone I know who freelances."
After a pause he said, "Home page is enough to launch. Thanks for telling me now."

qa.q: What had Aparna promised to build for Hrithik?
qa.a: She had promised to build the website for his tiffin service by Friday.

qa.q: What did Aparna feel when she looked at her calendar, and why?
qa.a: She felt her stomach drop, because the new office deadline meant she couldn't keep her promise to Hrithik.

qa.q: Which parts of Aparna's call made the change of plan work?
qa.a: She called early, owned the impact on his launch, and offered a clear smaller promise plus a backup, instead of vanishing or making vague excuses.

qa.q: How might Hrithik have felt if the message had come on Friday night instead?
qa.a: He would likely have felt let down and stuck, with his launch planned and no time to find another option.

grounding: When a promise can no longer be kept, a young woman says so early, owns the impact and offers what she truly can do.

Nitin, come and sit by your Dada Kishore. When I was ten, my friend Ramu told me he was scared of the dark and still slept with a lantern. "Swear you won't tell," he said. I swore. I felt so important, carrying that secret like a gold coin in my pocket. When boys called him a baby, I never said a word. It was heavy, but it was his.
Then one monsoon he whispered a different secret: he was going to swim across the swollen river to prove he wasn't a coward. My chest went tight. That night I told my father. He went straight to Ramu's house, and both fathers sat with Ramu till late. Ramu didn't speak to me for a week. But he was safe.

Counsellor's note, 22 August.
Uma (Class 10) came in at lunch, which she has never done before. Her class teacher had noticed her eating alone all week. Uma told me that in July she confided in Gurpreet that her parents were separating. Last week a group of girls asked her, in front of everyone, whether it was true her father had "left". She realised Gurpreet had told them.
She said, "I feel so stupid for telling anyone," and that she has stopped talking to all her friends, not only Gurpreet. She kept pulling her sleeves over her hands.
I told her that trusting someone is not stupid, and that the betrayal was not her fault. We agreed she will come on Thursdays for now. With her permission, I will ask her class teacher to change the group-work seating.

qa.a: Uma would still have someone to lean on during her parents' separation, instead of eating alone and guarding herself with everyone.

Varun's family of five lived in one room above a tailoring shop, with a curtain for a wall. There was no door to close. So Varun, who was ten, asked his mother Madhuri for something small: the empty biscuit tin with a latch, and a padlock from the hardware store.
"What are you hiding?" his uncle joked from the mat.
